summary.text: A skeletally immature 15-year-old female presented with a 6-month history of moderate, atraumatic left proximal tibial pain worsened by walking and limiting daily activities. Examination showed an antalgic gait and a palpable, warm swelling of the proximal tibia with pain on ankle dorsiflexion, and imaging revealed a proximal tibial lesion measuring 7.6 × 3.0 × 3.6 cm.

Histopathological analysis demonstrated an osteofibrous dysplasia-like adamantinoma. Because of the lesion volume, cortical breach and risk of pathological fracture, a radical en-bloc resection was performed after external fixator placement with Steinmann pins, leaving a 9-cm diaphyseal defect, followed by insertion of a Precice bone transport nail, an osteotomy and locking of the nail before the temporary fixation was removed.

Pain was managed with a sciatic catheter for four days and then opioid reserves, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 8 on paracetamol and NSAIDs. Physiotherapy began immediately, and distraction osteogenesis started on postoperative day 8 and continued for 230 days with a transport distance of 8.5 cm. At six months a transport screw exchange was performed after audible blocking during distraction.

Radiographs confirmed complete consolidation at 18 months, and complete hardware removal was performed at two years. At two-year follow-up the patient had marked improvement, only occasional mild pain, a normal gait, full knee and ankle motion, residual lateral lower leg hypoesthesia, an estimated Musculoskeletal Tumor Society score of 28/30, and no tumor recurrence.
